title: Zechariah 7:1–14
context: In the fourth year of Darius, a delegation from Bethel asks the priests and prophets whether they should continue the fast of the fifth month. The LORD answers through Zechariah by asking whether their fasts in the fifth and seventh months over seventy years were truly for him. He recalls the message of the former prophets: execute true justice, show kindness and compassion, and do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the foreigner, or the poor. The ancestors refused to listen and made their hearts as hard as flint, so the LORD scattered them and the land became desolate. The fasts are commonly linked with events in Jerusalem’s fall, and these links are held with care. Shared ground: God values justice and a true heart above ritual.

verses.text: In the fourth year of King Darius, the LORD’s word came to Zechariah in the fourth day of the ninth month, the month of Chislev.
verses.arminianNotes:
In the fourth year of King Darius, on the fourth day of the ninth month, Chislev, the LORD’s word comes to Zechariah. The narrator gives a precise date.

Arminian readers see God speaking into a specific moment of the community’s life.
verses.reformedNotes:
The date is usually placed about two years after the night visions (compare 1:7), though exact conversion to modern calendars should be held with caution.

Reformed readers see God’s word anchored in history. Shared ground: God speaks to real people in real time.

verses.text: The people of Bethel sent Sharezer and Regem Melech and their men to entreat the LORD’s favor,
verses.arminianNotes:
The people of Bethel send Sharezer and Regem Melech with their men to entreat the LORD’s favor. A delegation comes.

Arminian readers see sincere seeking of God’s will about worship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Readers differ on how the names in this verse are to be understood and on whether Bethel is the sender or part of a personal name.

Reformed readers see the people seeking God. Shared ground: both traditions read this as an inquiry made in good faith.

verses.text: and to speak to the priests of the house of the LORD of Armies and to the prophets, saying, “Should I weep in the fifth month, separating myself, as I have done these so many years?”
verses.arminianNotes:
They ask the priests and prophets, “Should I weep in the fifth month, separating myself, as I have done these so many years?” The question concerns a fast.

Arminian readers see a practical question about worship after restoration.
verses.reformedNotes:
The fifth-month fast is commonly linked with the burning of the temple (2 Kings 25:8–9; Jeremiah 52:12–13, which differ on the day).

Reformed readers see a question about worship. Shared ground: both traditions take the question seriously.

verses.text: Then the word of the LORD of Armies came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The word of the LORD of Armies comes to Zechariah. The answer begins, though not in the form the delegation expected.

Arminian readers see God addressing the heart behind the question rather than only the ritual detail.
verses.reformedNotes:
The reply unfolds over chapters 7–8 and is only directly answered in 8:19.

Reformed readers see God’s word reshaping the people’s concerns. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God answering a question about worship by turning attention to the heart and to justice.

verses.text: “Speak to all the people of the land and to the priests, saying, ‘When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and in the seventh month for these seventy years, did you at all fast to me, really to me?
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks whether, when they fasted in the fifth and seventh months for seventy years, they truly fasted “to me, really to me.” Arminian readers see motives examined.

Ritual alone is not enough.
verses.reformedNotes:
The seventh-month fast is often linked with Gedaliah’s murder (2 Kings 25:25; Jeremiah 41:1–2), though the text does not say so. Compare the seventy years of 1:12.

Reformed readers see God searching the heart. Shared ground: worship must be directed to God.

verses.text: When you eat and when you drink, don’t you eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks whether, when they eat and drink, they do not do it for themselves. Feasting, like fasting, can be self-centered.

Arminian readers see daily life as well as ritual brought under God’s claim.
verses.reformedNotes:
The question parallels the previous verse, applying the same test to eating as to fasting.

Reformed readers see the heart’s tendency to make religion self-serving. Shared ground: both traditions read this as a call to live and worship before God rather than for oneself.

verses.text: Aren’t these the words which the LORD proclaimed by the former prophets when Jerusalem was inhabited and in prosperity, and its cities around her, and the South and the lowland were inhabited?’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks whether these are not the words proclaimed by the former prophets when Jerusalem and its towns, the South, and the lowland were inhabited and prosperous. History speaks.

Arminian readers see the people invited to learn from the past.
verses.reformedNotes:
“The former prophets” likely refers to prophets before the exile, whose call to justice is summarized in verses 9–10.

Reformed readers see continuity in God’s word. Shared ground: both traditions read this as a reminder that God’s demands had been made clear before.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to Zechariah, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s word comes to Zechariah again. The message turns to what the former prophets said.

Arminian readers see God repeating his call so that the returned community will not repeat the failures of their ancestors.
verses.reformedNotes:
The renewed introduction marks a summary of earlier prophetic teaching.

Reformed readers see God’s word repeated for the people’s good. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God patiently restating his requirements to a new generation that has returned from exile.

verses.text: “Thus has the LORD of Armies spoken, saying, ‘Execute true judgment, and show kindness and compassion every man to his brother.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD of Armies says, “Execute true judgment, and show kindness and compassion every man to his brother.” Justice and mercy are joined.

Arminian readers see the heart of covenant faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
This summary echoes many earlier prophets’ calls to justice and mercy.

Reformed readers see the moral law reflecting God’s character. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God’s enduring call to justice and compassion, which outweighs ritual such as fasting.

verses.text: Don’t oppress the widow, the fatherless, the foreigner, nor the poor; and let none of you devise evil against his brother in your heart.’
verses.arminianNotes:
“Don’t oppress the widow, the fatherless, the foreigner, nor the poor,” and let no one devise evil against his brother in his heart. The vulnerable are protected.

Arminian readers see justice reaching both action and intention.
verses.reformedNotes:
The four groups named are often singled out in the law and the prophets as needing protection.

Reformed readers see God’s concern for the weak. Shared ground: both traditions read this as clear and lasting teaching on justice for the vulnerable and purity of heart.

verses.text: But they refused to listen, and turned their backs, and stopped their ears, that they might not hear.
verses.arminianNotes:
But they refused to listen, turned their backs, and stopped their ears. The response was rejection.

Arminian readers see a deliberate, chosen refusal of God’s word by the generation before the exile.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse describes the ancestors who heard the former prophets.

Reformed readers see the hardness of the human heart. Shared ground: both traditions read this as a sober account of how God’s people resisted his word, with real consequences that followed.

verses.text: Yes, they made their hearts as hard as flint, lest they might hear the law and the words which the LORD of Armies had sent by his Spirit by the former prophets. Therefore great wrath came from the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They made their hearts as hard as flint,” lest they hear the law and the words the LORD sent “by his Spirit by the former prophets.”

Arminian readers see hearts hardened by choice.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse links the prophets’ words to God’s Spirit.

Reformed readers see hearts needing God’s renewal. On the hardened heart, see the box at Deuteronomy 10:16. Shared ground: wrath followed refusal.

verses.text: It has come to pass that, as he called and they refused to listen, so they will call and I will not listen,” said the LORD of Armies;
verses.arminianNotes:
“As he called and they refused to listen, so they will call and I will not listen,” said the LORD of Armies. Refusal is answered in kind.

Arminian readers see consequences matching the people’s refusal.
verses.reformedNotes:
The shift from “he” to “I” is abrupt; readers take it as the prophet’s summary moving into the LORD’s own words.

Reformed readers see God’s just response. Shared ground: both traditions read this soberly as a word about that generation’s judgment.

verses.text: “but I will scatter them with a whirlwind among all the nations which they have not known. Thus the land was desolate after them, so that no man passed through nor returned; for they made the pleasant land desolate.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD scattered them with a whirlwind among unknown nations, and the land was left desolate. The pleasant land became a waste.

Arminian readers see the exile as the result of the ancestors’ refusal to heed the prophets.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse looks back on the exile as a completed judgment.

Reformed readers see God’s justice in history. Shared ground: both traditions read this as a warning to the returned community not to repeat the past, which prepares for the promises of chapter 8.
